1x1 count. Males engaging in some early courtship display, groups of males following females around, surrounding solitary females, throwing heads up and back, making a chittering/mummur type noise, chasing away other males. Females would occasionally confront males, looking at them and raising up heads in a stiff type posture, causing the males to back off and retreat. I would say 75-80% of raft was just resting, heads tucked, while the other 20-25% was engaging in this behavior, and the majority of those were male with a few females being displayed to. Around 5-6 males would surround 1 female. I did observe a male and female swim away together side by side with a few males following them. Audio recordings not great due to ambient noises, but I did my best to record the mummuring noises they were making.

properties.Observation Details: A single bird was singing from the large stand of White Pines on the lower Cresheim Creek, but was not seen. I first discovered this bird last year in this location, and it continues this year. Recording is attached...note the short duration of the song (not greater than 2 secs), about half the duration of a Chipping Sparrow's song---this is a feature that helps to distinguish the two species in the field. Also, this song was recorded in a pine forest with 100 yr-old trees and a dense shrub layer, quite distant and different from any yard where a Chipping Sparrow might be found.

properties.Observation Details: 1x1 count. Males engaging in some early courtship display, groups of males following females around, surrounding solitary females, throwing heads up and back, making a chittering/mummur type noise, chasing away other males. Females would occasionally confront males, looking at them and raising up heads in a stiff type posture, causing the males to back off and retreat. I would say 75-80% of raft was just resting, heads tucked, while the other 20-25% was engaging in this behavior, and the majority of those were male with a few females being displayed to. Around 5-6 males would surround 1 female. I did observe a male and female swim away together side by side with a few males following them. Audio recordings not great due to ambient noises, but I did my best to record the mummuring noises they were making.

properties.Observation Details:
Very rare, appears to be a potential third Pennsylvania record. First spotted/found by Ross, who then promptly alerted the rest of us, then well seen/heard by all for ~5 minutes after. 
 
 Obvious MOWA/MGWA-type, a large warbler with bright yellow coloration below extending from the throat through the under tail. Well defined blueish hood with a white throat, broad white eye arcs that were relatively short and bold, and a long appearing tail. Call note was a dry “chik”, seemingly a better match for MGWA than MOWA. The bird responded vigorously to MGWA call notes, coming in immediately and calling, and had no reaction to any MOWA call notes. 
 
 Thanks Ross!
 
 Pennsylvania #325

properties.Observation Details: As soon as I walked through the gate, I heard a YBCH singing loudly, which was unexpected given the time of day. I walked to the start of sparrow alley (on the path right next to the now dry pond) hoping to photograph the YBCH Patrick M. reported earlier. While trying to get a photo (which was challenging because it preferred perches deep in the brush), I realized there were 2 male YBCH, and one constantly was chasing the other from perch to perch. This behavior continued at a ferocious pace for over 20 minutes. Although I was remarkably close, they seemed largely oblivious to my presence. After 10-15 mins or so, I noticed a third bird flying in the opposite direction of the two battling YBCHs two separate times. Based on size & color, it appeared to be a third chat, not a COYE, but I couldn’t get any photos. Both times it flew low & straight into dense brush. Later, one of the YBCHs popped up further down sparrow alley on a branch next to the female INBU & did an incredible imitation of the INBU call. Pretty remarkable experience overall, & definitely a POD first for me. Photos & recordings.

I will not leave this entry as a mere Lorem Ipsum! Lo! Not even a mere tally! Instead I will pay homage to the  omnipresent meowing and kwüting of very visually obvious black grayish leaf turning dumetellaisimas . Groups of 2 to 7 at points of these darling mimics. Overcast and relatively cool today so the passerines including these munchkins were very active. The highest density was at the frog pond/poplar woods. But wait? What about the census results? Ah yes!...this was livelier than a Tiesto concert in an Amsterdam basement. about 75 partygoers on dike road, big boardwalk area , parking lot. 50-60 by the frog pond/poplar woods. The rest scattered around the woods between the boat launch and the visitor center. I suspected I heard young on nest with an adult seen nearby but didn’t see any obvious fledglings today . Soon there shall be many! One if not two birds were carrying food though . At one point several were mobbing something mercilessly. I have seen them go after a RSHA adult a bunch recently. Audio of the cat mob obtained as well as their standard repertoire of insistent feline irruptions. Oolala! Hail Catbird, We Who are About to Mew Salute You. 
 
 I have uploaded the following for your auditory delight. 
 
 Cat mob: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/586627381
 Standard catbird: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/586627771
 Advanced catbird (not too much different than standard catbird on this day!): https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/586628121
 Ultra hyper uber advanced red-eyed vireo mimicing catbird: TBC . To Be Catinued!

properties.Locality: stakeout MacGillivray's Warbler, W. Fort Mifflin Rd., Philadelphia (2023)
properties.Observation Details: Very rare, appears to be a potential third Pennsylvania record (previous two in Berks in 2004 and Dauphin in 2013, respectively), as well as representing a first Philadelphia County record. This keeps the trend of about one every ~10 years in Pennsylvania alive. First spotted/found by Ross, who then promptly alerted the rest of us of the presence of this intriguing bird, after which it was well seen/heard by all for ~5-10 minutes afterwards. An obvious MOWA/MGWA-type, a relatively large warbler, a HY bird in formative plumage by worn alula and primary coverts (as pointed out by ZM), with bright yellow coloration below extending from below the throat through the under tail. A tough species level identification given the superficial similarity to its congener MOWA, however all identification characteristics indicate MGWA. Pertinent identification points which favor MGWA include a complete, well defined blueish hood; completely grayish white/white throat with no yellow coloration; dusky gray band across the breast separating the dusky white throat from the yellow belly and vent; broad, abbreviated white eye arcs with abrupt edges (as opposed to sloping or tapered edges); a long appearing tail with visibly shorter undertail coverts than MOWA, and a dry chwit call note, which was recorded (see this recording for a comparison). Additionally, the bird responded vigorously to playback of MGWA call notes, coming in immediately, becoming agitated and calling in response. Conversely, the bird had no reaction to any playback of MOWA call notes. Timing obviously favors MGWA as well, as there are no November MOWA records on eBird for Pennsylvania and none after mid-October. This short guide by Pyle and Henderson is a very nice resource on separating the two closely related Geothlypis species in this plumage. Well documented with nice photos as well as some audio of the call notes.

I will not leave this entry as a mere Lorem Ipsum! Lo! Not even a mere tally! Instead I will pay homage to the  omnipresent meowing and kwüting of very visually obvious black grayish leaf turning dumetellaisimas . Groups of 2 to 7 at points of these darling mimics. Overcast and relatively cool today so the passerines including these munchkins were very active. The highest density was at the frog pond/poplar woods. But wait? What about the census results? Ah yes!...this was livelier than a Tiesto concert in an Amsterdam basement. about 75 partygoers on dike road, big boardwalk area , parking lot. 50-60 by the frog pond/poplar woods. The rest scattered around the woods between the boat launch and the visitor center. I suspected I heard young on nest with an adult seen nearby but didn’t see any obvious fledglings today . Soon there shall be many! One if not two birds were carrying food though . At one point several were mobbing something mercilessly. I have seen them go after a RSHA adult a bunch recently. Audio of the cat mob obtained as well as their standard repertoire of insistent feline irruptions. Oolala! Hail Catbird, We Who are About to Mew Salute You.

The spectrogram looks exactly like the first example of LOWA in Pieplow's 'Field Guide to Bird Sounds..' In quickly looking at examples in Birds of the World the spectogram actually looked closer to a  Northern, though not exactly. What bothered me about it being a NOWA was that what I recorded are two three note phrases following quickly upon one another, not the four or five note phrases generally seen in Northern, Those repeated 3 note phrases are exactly what Pieplow shows so I'm leaving this as a Louisiana.

properties.Observation Details:
Found adult male nest building. Flared tail coverts obvious. Then I thought I heard a Sapsucker. But it was the "whaaa" call of a female. Which turned out to be still in immature plumage (yearling). 
 BoNA notes for that call type: The whaaa call primarily by females, when flying toward males for food, during food exchanges between mates, when plucking prey delivered by males, and while flying back to nestlings with food, but not while feeding young at the nest. Before incubation, given in clusters of 1–4 notes, almost exclusively by females, when perched near males while latter nest-building, when in flight to or from nest, from perches preparatory to collecting twigs, but less so when loafing near nest while males away hunting. May be a non-aggressive or submissive signal of female's willingness to suspend potential for aggression and join in breeding, thus reassuring her smaller mate that it is not dangerous to be near her. May also function as a female food-begging call.
 
 I saw that nest during previous visits in the last few months and was wondering who it belonged to. Per BoNA 6-22% of breeding females are yearlings. Usually first breeding at 2 years of age.

properties.Observation Details: One singing an awful like a cerulean in the exact place where the cerulean was heard (I did not chase the Cerulean because I was enjoying a pleasant, non-stressful stroll and there was so much pishing when I got there).

*Rare. We were walking back towards the visitor center on haul road by the frog pond when I heard this bird singing and got our party’s attention. We listened for a couple minutes and I put the word out on the discord and the telegram. Soon after, the growing party of birders and I realized he was singing like crazy near the boat launch in the pipeline cut close to the original spot. We waited for a long time for him to show but he wouldn’t and was clearly in the canopy. I cannot rule out CERW x NOPA but now is peak Cerulean time and if I were in WV I wouldn’t think twice about listing a “heard only” Cerulean—their song rocks! Certainly it’s worth investigating mimicry by Parula and Cerulean and vice versa (I certainly will do more research—and there is evidence that the hybrids can sing both songs https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1440&context=ohio_cardinal) but this bird was persistently singing a couple variations (like this one I recorded in WV: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/619700015) of Cerulean for minutes on end . We did have a Parula singing at the same time as the cerulean from different directions but that’s pretty much to be expected in their breeding range. I have more audio to add . Sorry there’s talking. I was excited to say the least. Update 5/8 (1). I haven't found any evidence yet of Parula imitating Ceruleans. The song in my recording is a match for the song in this recording: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/635295399. The NOPAxCERW combo is extremely unlikely. It's at this point beyond reasonable doubt that this singer was a Cerulean. The song is clearly audible at 0:04, 0:19, and 0:38 in ML635238652: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/635238652 Update 5/8 (2): I did find an instance of Northern Parula not imitating per say but singing an atypical "odd" song somewhat similar to that of a Cerulean (...but two parted) at a specific site in Nebraska: "As Cerulean Warbler has declined in Nebraska in recent years, doubt has been raised by Justin Rink (personal communication) that heard only singers identified as Ceruleans at Indian Cave SP may in fact be Northern Parulas; all “odd” singers that might have been Ceruleans were tracked down and found by Rink to be Northern Parulas. Some or perhaps all of these “odd” songs may be an alternate Northern Parula song that Pieplow (2017) describes as a “second-category song”. This frequently heard two-part song consists of buzzy series of notes with the initial series lower in pitch than the succeeding series so sounds quite similar to a Cerulean’s song (Shari Schwartz, personal communication). On the other hand, “odd” songs do occur; one such singer, whose song consisted of a series of paired buzzes on the same pitch, was seen and heard in the same place at Indian Cave SP for two consecutive springs 2004 and 2005 (Paul Lehman, Ross Silcock; Silcock et al 2005)." Additionally, research has shown that the hybrids are able to sing atypical songs. I was able to access an article through the Penn Library which demonstrated with spectrograms the atypical song of a hybrid and noted it a couple cases the odd song lead to the detection of the hybrid. (Source: The Wilson J. of Ornithology, 131(3):615-624 (2019). https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1676/18-152) However, the bird heard at Heinz was singing a typical three part song of a Cerulean Warbler. It did not sound odd--the recordings sound completely normal for a Cerulean--and I had no reason to suspect it was a Parula singing. Given that Cerulean are rare but well documented as passage migrants at this time of year, I do not have reason to doubt the identification of this singer as a Cerulean--they have been recorded at Heinz this time of year as well. Feel free to examine this sighting thoroughly but I have no doubt about the identification.

I knew that this hab was good for this species and familiarized myself with it before today . State county patch bird . I am elated . I have previously found this species in Delaware and seen it in nj . Bird was here : 39.93340° N, 75.20956° W. It was affiliating with swamp sparrows at one point and at one point ...after I first encountered it ... it popped up in some prairie grass before flying a short distance. I was surprised to see this observation rejected without any communication. I believe the decision to do so was incorrect because Philadelphia is not in the hybrid zone and hybrids are not a material concern in the city of Philadelphia. As such I am submitting this record for re-review with details on the subject from the public work of Robert Curry and David Sibley.  For years, the Philly filter had hybrid chickadees not flagged as rare. This created a misconception that has probably led to a surprising number of undocumented reports. I too previously thought as a novice birder that hybrids could move. Recently though, the option for hybrid chickadee was flagged as rare in Philadelphia and there are no photo or genetic evidence-based documented reports of this combo.
 
 This article in Scientific American includes a map of the hybrid zone as of 2024, which has moved northward in Pennsylvania and New Jersey. The hybrids used to be absent from Hawk Mountain for instance per Curry's research but now the population there is mixed: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/hybrid-chickadees-reveal-how-species-boundaries-can-shift-and-blur/
 
 David Sibley, citing the well known hybrid researcher Robert Curry writes: "The actual isolating mechanism that prevents hybrids from spreading beyond the narrow contact zone could be as simple as the reduced fitness of hybrids. Curry reports that in Pennsylvania eggs of mixed pairs have a much lower hatching rate than those of pure pairs.” Source: https://www.sibleyguides.com/bird-info/black-capped-chickadee/black-capped-carolina-chickadee/
 
 The song and call of a black capped chickadee is not inate but the population of chickadees that would encounter both species and learn each other’s songs is sedentary.  As Sibley writes "In a narrow band from northern New Jersey to Kansas, however, Black-capped and Carolina Chickadee meet and hybridize. In that area, chickadees are essentially unidentifiable, and observers can only say that an individual bird “shows the characteristics of” one species or the other. Luckily, these populations are essentially sedentary, so hybrids are not a big concern away from the contact zone.” Additionally, Curry has proven that the hybrid zone is slowly shifting northward: https://homepage.villanova.edu/robert.curry/Documents/RLCpubs/Taylor.2014.evo12510.pdf
 
 The birds we see in Philly are coming from well north of the hybrid zone during irruption years. Sibley writes: "Black-capped Chickadees from the northern parts of the range stage periodic irruptive flights in fall, when hundreds or even thousands can be seen in a day flying past traditional migratory concentration points along the shores of the Great Lakes or the coast of New England. 
 
 Additionally, there have been documented and confirmed reports of Black-capped chickadees at Heinz and the across the city this winter, including before and after the date of this report.
 
 If there is a legitimate reason to reject the identification, I would like a written communication as to why with evidence included. If this is the case I would gladly change this identification but I don't believe this is the case. Thank you.
 -Ben FIlreis

I was recording a Cooper’s hawk in the meadow when I heard the bugles. I waited and there they were ! Coming from the lakes area going west. I counted 36 in the field but my video shows at least 32. They were going low over the meadow in two skeins pretty much right over me. Will revise upward if I can verify . This may very well be the new county high count . It’s a state/county bird for me and happens to be one of my favorite species for sure. Have observed this species in other states a fair amount particularly in Delaware and Florida. The birds were seen shortly thereafter at Heinz going southwest along the course of the river over the airport . Pics/audio/video to follow . Here’s a video I made of the birds: https://youtube.com/shorts/BGnRf_OvNtU?si=64Vm7oztiCWTVwVO.    
 
 Revised to 35 from 32 after reviewing pics of both skeins at home . The video cuts out a couple birds. I deliberately tried to get pics of both skeins and was thankfully able to do a decent job of doing so!
 
 Skein 1 had 20 birds: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/611436644
 Skein 2 had at least 15: note the I couldn’t fit the second skein in one photo but managed a couple burst shots of the group :
 See  https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/611444556 and https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/611444557
 
 Additional edit : looks like I did manage a pic of all 15 birds in the second skein!: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/611445374
 
 
 Note added 11.25.23 : I suspect that these birds are greater sandhill cranes. Look at the bills in this photo for instance: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/611436644 but would like better side profiles of the second skein . Changed the subspecies designation to tabida/rowani briefly but would like to research more before I make a call.

Stop one .05 miles in. 2 birds. Both tremolos and whinnies. One red morph seen . Another heard only . Stop two .25 miles into checklist . One maybe two birds giving kew calls heard and one tremoloing but creek bends so direct patch to first stop was close enough to skip . Still one probably was coming from a new direction from first two so maybe 3 total at this point in list. 
 
 Stop three .51 miles into list . >.2 miles direct distance to first stop (not accounting for trail bend). Two screech both Whinnies / tremolos. Saw whet type wail call heard before screech whinnies . I believe the screech was making a wail call because one of the wails had a tremulous end and soon after I heard a traditional whinny from roughly the same area. Listen to https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/594249131 for the wail calls (third wail into the recording is tremulous ) and then to hear the same wail calls followed shortly by whinnies: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/594251261. I trimmed the recording a bit but in real time the switch from wail to whinny happened in less than 2 minutes. Soon after, one screech seen silhouetted in flight / landed above me and subsequently calling keow and tremolos. (Note to self check recording 0021). One of the birds at the third stop made this (bark?) noise too: https://ebird.org/checklist/S144574037

I will not leave this entry as a mere Lorem Ipsum! Lo! Not even a mere tally! Instead I will pay homage to the  omnipresent meowing and kwüting of very visually obvious black grayish leaf turning dumetellaisimas . Groups of 2 to 7 at points of these darling mimics. Overcast and relatively cool today so the passerines including these munchkins were very active. The highest density was at the frog pond/poplar woods. But wait? What about the census results? Ah yes!...this was livelier than a Tiesto concert in an Amsterdam basement. about 75 partygoers on dike road, big boardwalk area , parking lot. 50-60 by the frog pond/poplar woods. The rest scattered around the woods between the boat launch and the visitor center. I suspected I heard young on nest with an adult seen nearby but didn’t see any obvious fledglings today . Soon there shall be many! One if not two birds were carrying food though . At one point several were mobbing something mercilessly. I have seen them go after a RSHA adult a bunch recently. Audio of the cat mob obtained as well as their standard repertoire of insistent feline irruptions. Oolala! Hail Catbird, We Who are About to Mew Salute You. 
 
 I have uploaded the following for your auditory delight.

 Advanced catbird (not too much different than standard catbird on this day!): https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/586628121

I was quite confident I heard HOLA giving tseep calls three times before I was recording. I texted the chatter thinking this is what I had. Then I heard a pipit and decided to leave horned lark off my list until lo and behold I picked one up while recording later. I recall scanning the area where the bird was the moment I heard this segment of the recording live (thinking pipit/lark at the time) and finding nothing. No mimics either in the area the bird was calling from. The call was coming from a patch of gravel and short grass just beyond the fence line at the southwest end of the soccer field (right where I’d expect to see a lark.) The bird appeared to fly in call and move on. So there may have very well been more than one bird. When you review this observation, note the slurred tee at 0:03-0:04 of my recording and some other vocalizations interspersed. Other notes: I consulted the following resource for identification: http://oldbird.org/pubs/fcmb/species/larks/hola/hola.htm  . Believe Frank had some records for this location , e.g. https://ebird.org/checklist/S11981745.

properties.Observation Details: Philly first for me!! At least two. Ran into Martin Selzer and we were talking about Woodcocks and one came flying in erratically behind him and landed behind a bush that was right in front of us. We started hearing "peent" calls and a minute later had one fly up for the display flight. My first one. Possibly close to us because one started "peenting" again and it was close. Did calls for a couple times and then stayed quite.

Audio file to be attached.  At Hoy's Pond, when I approached I heard a smattering of duck calls that sounded unfamiliar to me and not typical Wood Duck calls.  In particular there was no whiny aspect to the calls like typical calls.  I wasn't running Merlin and managed to scramble my phone out and turn it on, and got a snippet of the calls, though it doesn't do it justice (they were initially quite a bit louder).  I had an immediate reaction that Black-bellied Whistling-Duck came to mind.  Checking my Sibley v2 app after the fact, I thought it sounded quite close to the first audio example of their "phew' calls.  It did not correspond to any Wood Duck examples in that app.  Similar situation to example audio in Merlin app, though I can't say any of those sounded as close to the BBWD "phew" call.  In any case Merlin made no ID at the time of the recording.
 
 I didn't see any birds fly away, though they could have "snuck" out the corner obscured to my right.  I didn't get a sense from the calls that they were flying.  I moved around a bit and looked for anything other than Wood Ducks with no success.  Nor were any BBWD found in the impoundment!  There were and typically are, however, lots of eclipse plumage Wood Ducks in Hoy's Pond.  Given the preponderance of circumstantial evidence it seems likely these were just Wood Duck calls that were unfamiliar to me.

Careful count of westbound flyovers, by far the most common warbler we were able to identify in flight. Various plumages, some paler grayish and some yellow below with long thin streaks below, large white wing panels visible when seen at the right angle. Photos and recordings of several.

properties.Observation Details: Adding photos and audio recording which should nail down species.  Update: changing to Bicknell's instead of Gray-cheeked/Bicknell's based on some feedback from others, and looking at sonograms.  Although a little faint, the trilling at the end seems to always be at the higher frequency and never drops down low like G-c tends to do.

Flyover near waters edge, heard doubled pip-it call and slightly extended flight call which caught my attention. Attaching poor Merlin recording.  Difficult to hear but the signal is visible in the sonogram.

Heard sharp teew call (Cf. Sibley app nomenclature), with dropping pitch, very clearly at a relatively windless moment, looked up immediately and found a light-colored bird flying above and away. My first thought was Snow Bunting but the photos rule that out by lack of black wing tips and the dark undertail. I listened /compared to Sibley app recordings almost immediately for Snow Bunting and Horned Lark. Both have comparable calls to what I heard, to my ears, and are unlike other calls I’m more familiar with. Clean look underneath, nearly all dark under tail,  and apparent lack of streaking would rule out American Pipit, which generally has a doubled call in any case. Photos do seem to show light undertail coverts, very dark (under) tail feathers, but white outer tail feathers, all consistent with HOLA. Ground was snow-covered and very blue sky which noticeably made the numerous gulls appear unusually bright white which would also make this bird look very bright. No sign of dark collar but this could be due to angle. Attaching a snippet of recording with some hesitation, I did have Merlin app recording at the time but phone was in coat pocket and didn’t pick it up well. So short that you probably can't hear it unless you can loop it repeatedly, but the signal is visible in the sonogram.  Sonogram looks reasonable if not exactly definitive. HOLA has been reported in multiple locations regionally in the last few days, no doubt related to the snow cover.

Brief cuckoo chortle caught while recording for YB Chat. Merlin had suggested Black-billed. I have re-played it for merlin numerous times and each time it suggest Black-billed. I have also run it though BirdNET Sound ID which suggest both Black-billed and Yellow-billed. I was lucky enough to watch the female catch a mantis, take it apart, eat maybe a third of it and then carry the rest back to the bushes were the birds appeared from at the start. Even without this location being monitored over June/July I would consider this enough evidence that these birds are not migrants, but a territorial pair that actually might have bred here. Based on my experience with the very few breeding attempts since 2018 it is not unusual for juveniles to be attended by their parents in August when others might already migrate.

I was absolutely sure that I was hearing a Yellow-breasted Chat during 60 plus minutes of trying to locate it. The typical song of single notes separated by long pauses and then a long group of repeated notes was sung over and over again. Most noticeable was the long pause between both single notes and the repeated notes. I heard it at least 3 times for 3-5 minutes during 60 plus minutes. I was momentarily confused at the end of  the hour by a Northern Mockingbird that included one phrase show timbre was similar to that of the repeated call of the Chat. But later review of the six recordings I  made confirmed that it was a Yellow-breasted Chat.
 Since  it's taken a while to filter out the other closer bird calls, primarily one or more Common  Yellowthroats it's taken a while to post a good recording  here. It is not perfect  but  the Chat is  clear.
 There are four  types of notes or note phrases: 1, a whit-like upslur, found at 21, 33, 40,51, 56 and 118  seconds;  a second richer downslur at  02,08,18,29,35,39,52 and 102 seconds; a note phrase of just two repeated notes at seconds 06 and 25; and finally the more distinctive loud repeated notes, typical of  a Chat, at seconds  45-47.
 I'm removing the first audio I included and just leaving  the second because I think  it  is much clearer, especially if listened to while  looking  for the pattern described above.. If you look at the  sonogram you can actually predict when you'll hear the two most common single notes of this Chat song. Once  I got used to looking  at  it it was easy to predict when the next Chat  sound would be heard. I myself don't have the slightest doubt that it is a chat.

Soon after, one screech seen silhouetted in flight / landed above me and subsequently calling keow and tremolos. (Note to self check recording 0021). One of the birds at the third stop made this (bark?) noise too: https://ebird.org/checklist/S144574037

properties.Observation Details: Careful count . 3 maybe 4 at dawn moving (mostly upriver from roosts - perhaps migrants) then a pair then a couple flyovers (one going east then other across the river ) . one on nest in harbor that we excluded . It’s difficult to exclude which birds are local and whatnot but I tried to only count the ones that would leave our area of perception. Goofy long winged raptors with mostly white underparts excluding the primaries and other sections of the underwing . Flight style in the shape of an M. Peeping occasionally . This is a decent spot for migrant osprey movement as has been indicated in the past and it was a decent migration night before our watch at least for March .

Continuing since at least Jan 13th . Lots of buzzy indigo bunting like flight calls given. Affiliating with song and field sparrows. It behaves like some of the more skulky sparrows around here do . It jumped up low above the top of the long grass to check me out before diving into the brush only a foot away from its previous location. The bird would often check me out from behind cover . I observed it for 5 to 10 minutes or so , all while staying quiet and calm. I knew what it was as soon as it flushed. Tropical lime green chunky songbird larger and a lot less erratic than a kinglet and more vibrant than an orange crowned warbler.

properties.Observation Details: Heard same flight call as yesterday morning, this time flying east. A small shorebird-shaped bird was seen high in clouds to the east, backlit and distant, so just appeared dark. Unfortunately unable to discern any pertinant details. Similar in size to a Killdeer, but certainly not making any sound I’ve heard Killdeer make. Heard with Majorie and yelled for Ben who was on the east side of field to listen and he clearly heard it as well. Audio seems to match the recording I got on the previous morning. (https://ebird.org/checklist/S197015446)
Manny and Marjie have audio of its mournful calls as it flew over a bit before 7:30am. Really nice treat. Thanks Manny for picking it out and getting our attention.

Editing this to AMGP after hearing the same flight call the next morning (10/1) 
 
 Heard a distinctly different flight call then I am used to in the early morning. I was able to get a recording, albeit a poor recording, but it does seem to resemble the flight call of AMGP. I am not super familiar with their flight calls, so will trust the better judgement of the reviewers. 
 
 I’ve listened to a bunch of recordings online trying to compare to my recording and with Ben’s help he found one on this list in which the specs seem to match up the best: https://shorturl.at/Q6wwz  Sounding like a quick "tu-eee" or "pewy"  in the field, multiple calls were heard and they were spaced 4-5 seconds apart, the calls on both recordings occur at the same frequency (3-3.5kHz), same with the call I recorded the next day.
 
 In considering other possibilities, there have been a couple Starlings and Mockingbirds around, but neither species has been super vocal lately, Starlings have been quietly chattering and NOMOs have been mostly doing their “chewk” calls. Last year I found an AMGP at Penrose and briefly heard it in flight, at the time went over the calls of PAGP and EUGP to eliminate those possibilities (https://ebird.org/checklist/S148905548) again this call does not seem to match those species either. BBPL calls are longer sounding, whistle like calls, which did not match these.  There have been some Killdeer flyovers lately but did not sound similar to those. I did consider juvenile LAGU as there were a good number of them flying around in the morning and they seem to make some weird calls, but looking at recordings, their calls are more monotone and appear to have a long horizontal spec on a higher frequency too.

Saw it reported on eBird by Alexander G so went to go check it out with Tanya and was in same spot at end of environmental center parking lot by the meadow. It was drumming often and kept chasing Red-bellied Woodpeckers that were nesting nearby every time they came in with food it would chase them. Called couple times as we were getting ready to leave. It looked like maybe a first year as the back has slight scalloping showing and head was bright red but had some darker patches like it was just fully coming in. Looked like the bird was possibly setting up a territory and trying to attract a mate. Also at one point a Baltimore Oriole came flying to some Tulip Tree flowers to drink nectar and next thing the woodpecker was doing the same thing. Went to couple different flowers on the Tulip Tree. Pics/video/audio to upload. Seen with Tanya and Marty.

Brief cuckoo chortle caught while recording for YB Chat. Merlin had suggested Black-billed. I have re-played it for merlin numerous times and each time it suggest Black-billed. I have also run it though BirdNET Sound ID which suggest both Black-billed and Yellow-billed. I also reached out to a few experienced birders for feedback and they have agreed with/heard a Black-billed chortle. The more I listen to it the more confused I get. It does seem lower sounding than Yellow-billed. It is at the 2 second mark of the clip. Bird was not seen or heard again after hearing call. In the area where the YB Chat has been.  1st recording is full clip, 2nd recording is shorter version with volume boosted. (Audio)
 
 *First listed as cuckoo sp. but after some consideration, lots of listening to cuckoo calls, and reaching out to a few people, I am going to list it as Black-billed, as it sounds more akin to Black-billed than Yellow-Billed. Can change back to cuckoo sp. if recording is lacking enough of the call to be conclusive.

NFC 2. First listed as HETH but changed to RBGR.
 
 Original notes: "NFC 2. Appears to be the earliest fall county record (and only the second for August) by a few days. Feedback welcome as always...especially since thrushes have aberrant calls but this feels like the right id."
 
 __________________________________________________________________________________________
 
 Changed to passerine sp following day (8/21) . JG suggested maybe rosebeak!     
 _________________________________________________________________
 
 Updated again 8/21 to rosebeak NFC 2. The second call sounds just fine for rosebeak doing a hermit-thrush-esque call . The second one is pretty clearly burry (HETH is pure-toned) and both are slightly shorter in duration than many of the HETH example calls . It also appears to be rising then descending. This combined with the date (99.9999% probability by date it's a HETH over RBGR) has me convinced beyond reasonable doubt it's a rosebeak. 
 
 Per Evans/O'Brien: Rose-breated grosbeak will sometimes give "Pure-toned calls similar to Hermit Thrush but shorter, usually with a slight burry quality, and often more abrupt."

Changed to bird sp from puma after texting a friend for advice. Notes : “Was unsure whether to list this at first. Was standing in the parking lot near the ball fields looking at barn swallows when I heard a couple series of PUMA calls (from at least one bird maybe more) and recorded one of those (see attached). I thought it was above me was looked up and couldn’t spot the bird. There were a couple mockers but I don’t think they were integrating these calls into their repertoire and my impression in the field was it sounded like maybe more than one bird. (You can hear the Martin calls in the first ten seconds of the recording.) The mocker would mix in some of what sounded like an orchard oriole and barn swallow but only partial sequences of those two species and interspersed with its usual song notes. The calls I recorded on the other hand seem to be independent and I heard them more than once so I think it’s reasonable to assume I had at least one Martín. “

properties.Observation Details: *Rare. We were walking back towards the visitor center on haul road by the frog pond when I heard this bird singing and got our party’s attention. We listened for a couple minutes and I put the word out on the discord and the telegram. Soon after, the growing party of birders and I realized he was singing like crazy near the boat launch in the pipeline cut close to the original spot. We waited for a long time for him to show but he wouldn’t and was clearly in the canopy. I cannot rule out CERW x NOPA but now is peak Cerulean time and if I were in WV I wouldn’t think twice about listing a “heard only” Cerulean—their song rocks! Certainly it’s worth investigating mimicry by Parula and Cerulean and vice versa (I certainly will do more research—and there is evidence that the hybrids can sing both songs https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1440&context=ohio_cardinal) but this bird was persistently singing a couple variations (like this one I recorded in WV: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/619700015) of Cerulean for minutes on end . We did have a Parula singing at the same time as the cerulean from different directions but that’s pretty much to be expected in their breeding range. I have more audio to add . Sorry there’s talking. I was excited to say the least. Update 5/8 (1). I haven't found any evidence yet of Parula imitating Ceruleans. The song in my recording is a match for the song in this recording: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/635295399. The NOPAxCERW combo is extremely unlikely. It's at this point beyond reasonable doubt that this singer was a Cerulean. The song is clearly audible at 0:04, 0:19, and 0:38 in ML635238652: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/635238652 Update 5/8 (2): I did find an instance of Northern Parula not imitating per say but singing an atypical "odd" song somewhat similar to that of a Cerulean (...but two parted) at a specific site in Nebraska: "As Cerulean Warbler has declined in Nebraska in recent years, doubt has been raised by Justin Rink (personal communication) that heard only singers identified as Ceruleans at Indian Cave SP may in fact be Northern Parulas; all “odd” singers that might have been Ceruleans were tracked down and found by Rink to be Northern Parulas. Some or perhaps all of these “odd” songs may be an alternate Northern Parula song that Pieplow (2017) describes as a “second-category song”. This frequently heard two-part song consists of buzzy series of notes with the initial series lower in pitch than the succeeding series so sounds quite similar to a Cerulean’s song (Shari Schwartz, personal communication). On the other hand, “odd” songs do occur; one such singer, whose song consisted of a series of paired buzzes on the same pitch, was seen and heard in the same place at Indian Cave SP for two consecutive springs 2004 and 2005 (Paul Lehman, Ross Silcock; Silcock et al 2005)." Additionally, research has shown that the hybrids are able to sing atypical songs. I was able to access an article through the Penn Library which demonstrated with spectrograms the atypical song of a hybrid and noted it a couple cases the odd song lead to the detection of the hybrid. (Source: The Wilson J. of Ornithology, 131(3):615-624 (2019). https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1676/18-152) However, the bird heard at Heinz was singing a typical three part song of a Cerulean Warbler. It did not sound odd--the recordings sound completely normal for a Cerulean--and I had no reason to suspect it was a Parula singing. Given that Cerulean are rare but well documented as passage migrants at this time of year, I do not have reason to doubt the identification of this singer as a Cerulean--they have been recorded at Heinz this time of year as well. Feel free to examine this sighting thoroughly but I have no doubt about the identification.

Then I heard a pipit and decided to leave horned lark off my list until lo and behold I picked one up while recording later. I recall scanning the area where the bird was the moment I heard this segment of the recording live (thinking pipit/lark at the time) and finding nothing. The call was coming from a patch of gravel and short grass just beyond the fence line at the southwest end of the soccer field (right where I’d expect to see a lark.) Messy bib white hockey sticks etched into secondaries and upperwing coverts buffy flanks slower dee dee dee calls . Point blank looks at the three of them together eye level with a Carolina next to them hanging out a bit north of the recycling center . Another three together about .5 miles away . Got to look closely at all six birds over the course of a few minutes for each group. Wish I had more time I could have gotten more I bet . Usual spot . Two large thick billed corvids affiliating closely seen for a while . Communicating with each other with some strange noises that were much more complex then the usual croaks . At a couple points, I thought I heard croaks etc from three different directions while I was looking at two birds as if the third was obscured. Then all of a sudden the two birds flew around and a two more appeared. Didn’t see any obvious size difference between the 4 corvids or all seemed to be affiliating and flew off in the same direction at the same time ….Upping this to 4 from 3 ravens and one crow/raven sp based review of photos and behavior. One of my photos has all four birds. One is on the left of the image near the brick chimney (?) two next to each other and a fourth on the right. The one on the right is shown better in the second image. Usually when a crow is around a pack of ravens it’s not happy and these birds seemed content with each other. I heard lots of raven calls but no other corvids when viewing these birds.

properties.Observation Details:
Philly #255  . Around 7:34am , I spotted a lone snow bunting in flight upriver a bit on the NJ side. I watched it as it flew directly across from me at the east end of the admiral Peary blvd. It was flying quite low--low enough so I could see its upperwings and pale underparts. The bird came fairly close at one point and almost reached Pa water . It was flying with long shallow undulations. It showed distinctive white and black wing patches , and gave few low pitched rattle calls with a strong rising component and dozens of sweet sounding tew calls . I watched it over the course of three to four minutes and heard it for a couple of those minutes . I was recording at the time but I was worried my voice recorder app on my iPhone sitting on the roof of my car wouldn’t pick it up so I grabbed it and did manage a decent recording of its tew calls but not the rattles. I have photographed and recorded this species before and am 100% sure of this observation: https://media.ebird.org/catalog?taxonCode=snobun&userId=USER1912212 . Later in the day, I learned that 6 snow buntings were seen at Dream Park, Gloucester NJ, just a bit downriver from the navy yard.
 
 Additional notes: there have been 3 recent reports of this species in the last month in this area. There was some fog this morning but thankfully not too much and there was enough decent lighting for me to see this bird. You’ll have to crank the volume up for the recordings. My third recording shows the spectrogram fairly well. The first has a little volume boost. The second has a pass filter and the third has that and a 3 band EQ. The clearest spectrogram is in the third recording. I have previously read this resource about longspur/snow bunting rattles and find it quite useful for those looking to observe this species here again: http://oldbird.org/pubs/fcmb/species/longspur/rattles.htm

It was flying quite low--low enough so I could see its upperwings and pale underparts. The bird came fairly close at one point and almost reached Pa water . It was flying with long shallow undulations. It showed distinctive white and black wing patches , and gave few low pitched rattle calls with a strong rising component and dozens of sweet sounding tew calls . I watched it over the course of three to four minutes and heard it for a couple of those minutes . I was recording at the time but I was worried my voice recorder app on my iPhone sitting on the roof of my car wouldn’t pick it up so I grabbed it and did manage a decent recording of its tew calls but not the rattles. I have photographed and recorded this species before and am 100% sure of this observation: https://media.ebird.org/catalog?taxonCode=snobun&userId=USER1912212 . Later in the day, I learned that 6 snow buntings were seen at Dream Park, Gloucester NJ, just a bit downriver from the navy yard.
 
 Additional notes: there have been 3 recent reports of this species in the last month in this area. There was some fog this morning but thankfully not too much and there was enough decent lighting for me to see this bird. You’ll have to crank the volume up for the recordings. My third recording shows the spectrogram fairly well. The first has a little volume boost. The second has a pass filter and the third has that and a 3 band EQ. The clearest spectrogram is in the third recording. I have previously read this resource about longspur/snow bunting rattles and find it quite useful for those looking to observe this species here again: http://oldbird.org/pubs/fcmb/species/longspur/rattles.htm

properties.Observation Details: Crazy experience. Sitting in my couch and catch a huge ball of small birds just as they passed my window heading north up my street. I ran down with my puppy to walk up the street and it was pretty quiet for bird song. Walked up the next block and crossed the street to walk back down and halfway down the block I heard one zheee call and looked up and the flock of Siskin were all right above me feeding on Hemlock cones. Pretty quiet while feeding and couple made calls while flying off. The rest stayed and kept feeding until I left. I went back up with my birding neighbors Bernie and Amy but the birds were gone. We checked all the other Hemlocks on the two blocks as we are fortunate enough to have many but no luck finding them again. The Hemlock branching were literally fluttering with Siskin all over and you could see cone debris raining down from all the birds. Audio and bad iPhone video.

 The 1st year male was seen several times and was the singing the loudest and more frequently than the other. The other I only heard later and was singing more softly in close proximity to the other. I first heard the 1st year male singing distantly from the east of Ballard Brook. It eventually came closer and crossed over to the west side, and then went further towards the brush behind Thoreau's Hut. When it got there, I started hearing the second, seemingly singing in response to the other, but much more quietly.  I don't know if that counts as countersinging. Eventually they seemed to keep moving and went towards Pine Road and I think crossed over, or at least the 1st year male did. I'm not sure if the other one followed it or just stopped singing.

about 2½ hours of this checklist spent staking her out after initially sighting. got audio of her making a pip call several times but she evaded photographs. Rounded crown, crisp thin eye-ring, low contrast wing bars, and primary projection that was neither extensively long (acfl, ewpe) nor stubby (lefl) made me think this was most likely a traill's type. Pip call had no hint of ascending "whit", like a willow's occasionally given pip-alike might, and was given several times. Stuck mostly to the area around a denser thicket of trees and shrub by the stream between landsdown and horticultural drive (39.9818350, -75.2109674). Perched and hunted mainly middle to low understory, rotating around where initially spotted.

properties.Observation Details: Calling loudly near Kitchens Lane Bridge. I spooked a warbler sized  bird into the Japanese Knotweed which is nearly impenetrable in that way area and never saw him again. I’m pretty certain it was him. I made a few recordings and am including the best. It is 2 minutes long and waterthrush doesn’t start singing until 37th second but continues on from there. I left initial 37 seconds just to give context to the aural environment of the waterthrush. After ebird flagged this as a Northern rather as a Louisiana Waterthrush I spent a long time trying figure out why - though I have to say I no longer hear and see Louisianas  in the Philadelphia area with the regularity I used to. In any case the three louder slurred notes of Louisiana are missing here. I mistook the three sharper notes as them. Also the preceding notes were not as loud so It wasn’t clear to me that they were part of the song. But they are thus giving the regular 3-part rhythm of a Northern. The end notes however are more like a Louisiana, as also noted by Nathan Pieplow in his Field Guide to Bird Sounds. So there is some similarity to Louisiana but the lack of clear, slurred introductory notes should have alerted me to the fact that it wasn’t a Louisiana,

*Editing this to AMGP. 
 
 In the early morning as I was walking the field on the east end of the Navy Yard I heard a bird making some soft calls in flight. I was unable to get a visual on the bird, but I did have my merlin app running and it suggested Semipalmated Plover. 
 
 I am not very proficient in flight calls, and in the field it superficially resembled the calls of  SEPL I've heard at Heinz enough that I lazily just listed it as such.
 
 Upon further listening and looking at the spectrogram, I began to question my initial impression. I think the call is maybe too long for an SEPL call? Other recordings of SEPL calls in the Macauley Library seem much quicker and sharper sounding...not as drawn out as this one. While both calls are described as "whistled" in BoW, their description of the SEPL call is "a soft, clear, vigorous, whistled tyoo-eep, kerwee, or chu-wheet" and further says their flight call sound like a "quickened version of common call" I would not describe the call I heard as vigorous or clear. This bird was flying over, so I would think it would also sound and appear quicker in the spectrogram, which it does not to my untrained ear and eye. This was a softer more mournful “pwee”, with a longer looking spectrogram (especially the second part)
 
 Nathan Pipelow, in his guide on bird sounds does mention that these calls can be quite plastic in both species...so I could be totally wrong on this. The more times I listen to my recording the more confused I get.
 
 Last year I had the same issue with an unfamiliar call at the end of Sept. (https://ebird.org/checklist/S197015446) and the spectrograms appear similar (although this current recording is much worse) which makes me lean towards AMGP as the possible correct ID. 
 
 Since AMGP is not very common in Philadelphia and my experience with them and their calls extremely limited I will again lean heavily on the expertise of the reviewers. Will gladly amend this if it is an SEPL or if the recording is not adequate for an ID. (And maybe one day I’ll learn these calls better!) 
 
 Attaching two recordings, the second one has additional high pass filter.

Heard repeatedly along haul road and a little later on the power line cut opposite the original spot. Song seemed to be coming from the leafed out treetops and we never could see it, which is often typical of behavior for this species. Song was in 3 parts, with each part rising in pitch : starting with a couple longer notes, then a higher faster series of notes, ending with an even higher buzzy note. Tone of all 3 parts was buzzy. A parula was also present and singing for comparison.  Several recordings added, more are available if needed.

I did not expect that to happen in this ATV-stricken tract of woods. I first heard a bird singing, which was surprising enough. Then, I saw another one close to the singer. And then I heard a second singer a bit farther away. The second bird only called and generally stayed in the same small, fern-covered patch. So, I decided to come back later with better lighting.
 An hour later, the same setup was still in place: one adult singing, another only chiming in once in a while, and a third adult in the same patch as before. I waited, and a few minutes later, there was some movement under the ferns. It was hard to see, but it was a fledgling! As much as I could see, it was fairly non-descript brown, maybe half the size of the adult. As the female moved around, the little one followed with a mix of hopping (walking?)/fluttering.

 Above are my live field notes. Got home and listened to the recording. Zeep flight call complex. Presumed yellow makes sense.

Started below Blue Bell and worked north, stopping every 1/4 mile, per our usual protocol. Stop 1: 1 bird. One heard tremoloing Stop 2: 1 bird. One heard whinnying and then gray morph adult seen maybe diff bird Stop 3: one heard calling : bark call with a tremolo ending similar to https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/594238501 Stop 4: 2 birds juvenile red morph - red bodied with a fuzzy dull gray colored  head and one tremoloing simultaneously Stop 5 : 1 bird whinnying Stop 6: two birds simultaneously making bark keow and tremolos  . Stop 7: 3 birds whinnying and tremoloing . Thermal used to pick out one and  another flew right over BF . Stop 8: 1 making tremolous keow calls Stop 9: 3 birds from different directions whinnies and tremolos Stop 10: 2 birds . One doing whinnies and tremolos and another doing the tremolous bark thing Stop 11: 1 doing whinnies and tremolos . stop 12: 2 birds whinnies and tremolos . One was an adult red morph .stop 13 : one bird whinnying stop 14 : 2 birds whinnying one was a gray morph adult  stop 15: two birds seen and heard whinnies and tremolos  . One was grayish brownish . BF initially thought brown morph . The other was seen in flight poorly but tremoloing just the same . Stop 16: one maybe two  doing the bark call with a tremulous end and whinnies and tremolos  stop 17: two tremoloing and one tremoloing and whinnying stop 18: two birds wailing and then doing traditional screech whinnies and such  . Stop 19: two birds whinnies and tremolos . Stop 20: two bird: whinnies and tremolos. Stop 21 . Two birds  whinnies and tremolos plus a juv calling (like a screech hissing).       
 
 Update( 07.21.23 ): Bear with me . Have recordings to upload in the near future. the usual vocalizations as I recall ; nothing unusual .
 
 P.S. I think you can up the filter from 2 for this species to at least 3 or 4. The filter for GHOW is tripped at 4 and 3 for screech? Not sure why the difference. Especially this time of year when it's normal to encounter family groups and screech are a very common owl and lots around in certain areas of Philly. Just hardly anyone looking this time of year.

properties.Observation Details:
Continuing in second horseshoe just south of obs deck  . We heard chit chitting then BF spotted a nice skulky wren with pale supercilium and throat with light colored underparts and chestnuty upperparts in reeds . The bird was facing me so I couldn’t see its flanks easily or white stripes on back but it is clear what it is….The image in this hyperlink is roughly akin to the view of the bird I had (https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/552405761)
 
 The call in my recording (note the three chits in the first few seconds as well as more chits sporadically later) is a match for Marsh Wren from Pennsylvania. Here is a an example recording of a marsh wren giving a similar call:
 https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/519600481
 ...and here's a similar example from NJ: https://macaulaylibrary.org/asset/518153301.
 
 I knew by the call it was a marsh wren and it was very clear just by looking at it was not any other type of wren but sedge or marsh. 
 
 How I ruled out other wrens instantly after seeing it:
 House - wrong call, too strong a supercilium , wrong overall color.
 Carolina - wrong call, wrong coloration on upper part , and underparts , skulky habitats of hiding in the reeds vs the inquisitive nature of Carolina.
 Winter - wrong everything. color, call, etc.
 Sedge wren - call type, wrong coloration of supercilium, crown.

08.07.23 update: Changing this from 14 to X. I'm certain we had at least one saw whet owl just based on the law of probability coupled with the recordings attached that are suggestive of this species and some would argue appropriate for an id. .            .....Exact count. Audio recording of several of them. Tally, all widely separated except two at the same spot just south of Valley Green Inn. All were giving squeal calls. The call varied somewhat as is typical for this species in the fall. (Listen to recordings.) Pretty incredible experience. Highlight was hearing two at once. It was much easier to hear these birds than any previous night I’ve been to the Wiss since there was virtually no wind. Used point count method to which Chris alluded.  Amazing! Calling from a young stand of cattails. Initially, we were thinking Clapper Rail, but when we accidentally flushed the bird it was brown instead of the expected gray. In the end, it came even outside and the coloration was obvious. So was the clear border of the black-and-white flanks and the chest (as opposed to washed out). Calling frequency also seems to be in line with 2-3 keks per second as opposed to 4-5/s. Last record in Philly at Heinz in 2013 and 1999. Apparently used to breed there in the 1950s.

The male was singing sporadically from perches about 7-10m away from the fledglings' shrub, and the female was skulking nearby giving scolding "chatter" calls. One of the fledglings also gave a scolding call, much like the adult. The fledgling's calls were recorded on my microphone.
